headline: "Let them take out LA." California's leaders answered.
summary: At a Nebraska rally on Monday, Trump said the gas prices from the war with Iran were a small price for keeping the world safe. Then: "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." Governor Newsom called him deranged and dangerous. Both mayors objected. The White House says he meant a nuclear Iran would have threatened them.
cover_answer: He said it. His staff say he meant Iran was the threat.
table_question: Your words came out wrong and hurt someone. Say sorry, or explain?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president made a speech about the war with Iran and said something about two cities in California that sounded like he wanted them hurt. The grown-ups who run those cities got angry, and his helpers say he meant the opposite. Like a joke that comes out mean and makes the room go quiet. Nothing happened to any city.
5-7.why: Shielded: a child this age cannot do anything with a threat to a city. If it reaches them, nothing happened is the script.
5-7.why_long: Cantor's work on fright says a young child takes the vivid physical threat for the whole event, and a president saying a city could be taken out is exactly that, so a parent does not raise it. If it arrives, the script gives them one thing to hold: words at a speech, and nothing happened to any city. Expect "is our town next?" No.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: At a Nebraska rally, Trump called the war's gas prices a small price for safety, then: "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." California's leaders called it a threat. His staff say he meant Iran was the danger. A referee's replay: the words are on tape, the fight is over meaning.
8-12.why: The quote is on the tape, the fight is over meaning. The replay is theirs.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults apply them to themselves, and the script hands them the test: the words are on the tape, the speaker says they meant something else. The referee's replay is a mechanism they use at every game. Expect "why would he say that?" The quote and his staff's explanation are all anyone has.

13-17.script: When a president says "let them take out Los Angeles," does what he meant count more than what he said? The White House says he meant the threat from a nuclear Iran. Second: parts of the crowd cheered. What does that tell you?
13-17.why: Intent against plain text: a fight teenagers already have about their own words.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the sentence a president said out loud, and the meaning his staff say it carried. The script puts both in front of them and asks which counts, then asks about the cheering, which neither side disputes. Expect "would you accept that excuse from me?" Turn it round: would they accept it from him.

5-7.q: Did something happen to those cities?
5-7.a: No. Words at a speech. The people who run the cities got angry.

8-12.a: He said it. His staff say he meant a danger Iran would have been.

8-12.q: Why does gas cost more because of a war?
8-12.a: Trump calls higher prices a cost of the Iran war, and a small one.

13-17.q: Does what he meant beat what he said?
13-17.a: That is the fight. The quote is on tape; the explanation came after.

13-17.q: Why does it matter that the crowd cheered?
13-17.a: Parts of the crowd cheered, the BBC says. Threat heard, or point taken?

caption:
He said it. His staff say he meant Iran was the threat.

At a Nebraska rally on Monday, Trump said the gas prices from the war with Iran were a small price for keeping the world safe. Then: "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." Governor Newsom called him deranged and dangerous. Both mayors objected. The White House says he meant a nuclear Iran would have threatened them.
